chapter_theme: Saccandan consoles Vijayai with the countless births and two-day kinship of the Jina's teaching and sends her off in the peacock machine; then, alone against Kattiyankaran's army, he slays elephants, is pierced by discus and spear, and dies, and the narrator mourns the just sceptre swallowed by the minister-snake while the king goes as guest to the gods and his women wail.

cast.role: Saccandan's minister, given the rule, who usurps it
Kattiyankaran's warriors who besiege the palace
the king's five hundred women who lament him

270.reading: The king tells the queen that their past births, counted, outnumber the sands of the shore, that in all of them they were born strangers and parted, that in the states of birth to come they will not stay joined, and that kinship in a household is a matter of two days, not to be mourned.
270.nuance: கதிகள் is the word for the states of rebirth that the Jain teaching counts as four; the verse itself does not number them, but 271 at once grounds the consolation in the Jina's scripture. The argument from countless births is used here not to urge renunciation but to stop a wife's grief at parting.

claims.claim: one's past births are beyond counting, more than the sands of the shore
in the states of birth (கதிகள்) beings pass through, those joined now meet as strangers and do not stay together
kinship within a household lasts two days and should not be grieved

271.reading: He tells her that she, who has as if drunk in and stored the subtle scripture made by the Jina of the bee-loud asoka, should not become like one without understanding, sobbing with tears streaming; it does not befit her, and she must let her care go.
271.nuance: The Jina is named by the பிண்டி, the asoka, the same tree whose fall in Vijayai's dream (223) foretold the king's death, so the consolation is drawn from the emblem of the very loss it consoles.

claims.claim: one who has absorbed the Jina's subtle scripture should not grieve like one without understanding

272.reading: Like a young lion holding a fire-bright sword, he says that kings of glory do not go until they have sent their household ahead, that this is his duty too, that the vehicle is ready, and that she must not worry, for her going is what matters now.
272.nuance: உரிமை முன் போக்கி can mean sending the women away or sending them before one in death; here it is the queen's escape in the machine, and the clause tells her, without saying it, that he is going to die.
272.event: Saccandan tells Vijayai the vehicle is ready and she must leave before he goes.

claims.claim: a king of renown does not go to his end until he has sent his household ahead

273.reading: With love so great that his bones and heart seemed to melt, he speaks of the command of the lord of fame and sets his dear wife, unable to bear it, in the sorrowless bird-vehicle, and his companion goes in.
273.nuance: Whose command (இறைவனது ஆணை) he speaks of, his own as king or a vow by his god, the line does not settle. துன்பம் இல் பறவை ஊர்தி is the peacock machine of 235 to 239.
273.event: Saccandan places the grieving Vijayai in the peacock machine and she boards it.

274.reading: After the lady has gone, the tears from her long kuvalai eyes wetting her breasts, the noble prince turns red with fury and roars like a mass of fire burning up the earth's cold sea.
274.event: Vijayai departs in tears and Saccandan, enraged, roars.

275.reading: The warriors close round the prince like men hemming a roaring lion at a cave mouth; caught inside the wall of the palace, he is ringed in a sea of flashing swords and cloud-like elephants as in a flood.
275.event: Kattiyankaran's warriors and elephants surround Saccandan within the palace wall.

276.reading: Drawing his steel-forged sword in blazing wrath, with his shield of many hairs set with great gems, he whirls it like sunlight and roars like a bright-smiling god slipped down from the sky.
276.nuance: கயில் அணிக் கதிர் நகைக் கடவுள் is hard to construe; the god is unnamed.
276.event: Saccandan takes up sword and shield and roars.

277.reading: When the warriors have poured arrows like rain and shouted, the valiant prince wards off the hot arrow-rain and drives it back like the sea, and then the enemy army's great elephants close in upon him.
277.event: The warriors loose arrows; Saccandan beats them back, and the enemy elephants close in.

278.reading: The furious king drives his bloodied sword into the brow and tusk of the elephant that reaches him, and the musth elephants' frontal globes split like a spring-fed mountain struck by thunder.
278.event: Saccandan splits the attacking elephants' heads with his sword.

279.reading: Breaking the hedge of crowded spears, battering fierce warriors with his shield and cutting through the net of swords, he wades in blood, and the red field of the honey-garlanded king is at its height.
279.event: Saccandan breaks through spears, warriors and swords, wading in blood.

280.reading: Like the salt sea raging at its shore, the king, alone in an army equal to it, crushes great elephants; and in that army the lord, raging, drives his elephant forward, the sentence running into the next verse.
280.nuance: The அண்ணல் of the enemy army is not named until 285; that it is Kattiyankaran, who throws the discus and spear of 281 and 283, is a reading of the sequence, not stated.
280.event: Saccandan, alone, crushes elephants while the enemy lord drives his elephant at him.

281.reading: Raising the wheel kept close at hand, he cuts the shield through the middle, as the snake joins the running disc of the sun, whirling it with a rush, and rages more than a fire devouring a forest.
281.nuance: The image is of an eclipse, the snake meeting the sun; 290 turns it on the king himself. Whether the last line's rage is the thrower's or the king's is not clear.
281.event: The enemy lord's discus cuts the king's shield in two.

282.reading: His ghee-anointed sword with its blazing edge flashing, the king slays musth elephants in numbers and cuts one's trunk at the root so that it sinks; and the enemy lord cannot bear it.
282.nuance: அது நோனான் is taken as the foe's reaction, leading into his spear-throw in 283.
282.event: Saccandan's sword kills elephants, one with its trunk cut off; his foe cannot bear it.

283.reading: Raising a spear whose point flashes like lightning in cloud, he hurls it like Death into the king's handsome mountain chest, where the twin breasts of peacock-like women once slept, spoiling his spread garland.
283.nuance: The chest is described by the women it held: the pleasure that 261 blamed for the king's fall is recalled at the moment of his mortal wound.
283.event: The enemy lord hurls a spear into Saccandan's chest.

284.reading: Pulling out the white spear lodged in the wound of the chest where golden women's eyes had rested, he sets it between the tusks of an elephant fallen to earth and straightens its bent shaft, while warriors fill the sky.
284.nuance: விண் இடம் மள்ளர் கொள்ள may mean the watching warriors' cries filled the sky or that warriors died and took the sky; மிறைக்கொளி is obscure.
284.event: Saccandan draws the spear from his own wound and straightens it on a dead elephant's tusk.

285.reading: As the lord straightens the spear, the elephants flee and the sword-wielders shrink from him as from Death; when the warriors have given way, Kattiyankaran, fierce and brave, drives his elephant hard at him and scatters caltrops.
285.nuance: The narrator grants the usurper தறுகண் ஆண்மை, fierce courage, in the very line that names him.
285.event: The enemy breaks before the king; Kattiyankaran charges on his elephant, scattering caltrops.

286.reading: Knitting his brows like the great one who rode the crested peacock and split the mountain's chest with his white spear, he kills and fells Kattiyankaran's elephant, leaps onto another war elephant, and becomes the mark for all the great warriors standing there.
286.nuance: The simile is Murugan splitting the mountain, used freely in a Jain epic. நீள் முடி இலக்கம் ஆனான் may mean he became the target of all or stood foremost among crowned warriors.
286.event: Saccandan kills Kattiyankaran's elephant and mounts another.

287.reading: With weapons sunk in his chest, like the one who lies on the poison-filled serpent couch, he breaks the cloud-capped mountain shoulders of his foes, destroys great-footed elephants, and stands with his killing sword broken.
287.nuance: Line 1 names Vishnu on the serpent bed; whether he is the king's likeness or part of a compressed simile for the wounded chest is not clear.
287.event: Saccandan, wounded, fights on until his sword breaks.

288.reading: In the fierce battle the manly one, unblinking as the warriors' weapons rain on him, shines like the young one who once stood unretreating in the great war with his great father.
288.nuance: Who the young one fighting with or against his great father (பெருந் தாதை) is, the verse does not say; it points to a known story and I cannot fix it from the Tamil.

289.reading: Pierced by the bright discus and the spear, his fierce eyes still blazing, he falls so that the earth-goddess's breasts are pressed, and the manly one goes out like the setting sun.
289.nuance: The death is told as an embrace of the earth-goddess and a sunset: the king's last union is with the land he neglected.

290.reading: Men faint and women wail, the cruel sceptre spreads its darkness, alas the sin: the minister, a great snake, has swallowed Saccandan, lord of kings, the sun of the just sceptre risen from the deep sea of the Kuru line.
290.nuance: The narrator names only the minister's treachery here, calling the king அறச் செங்கோல், though 261 blamed his surrender to pleasure; the eclipse image of 281 returns with the minister as the snake. The first line's தோய்ந்த விசும்பு என்னும் தொல் நாட்டு அகம் is compressed.
290.event: The kingdom mourns as the minister's cruel rule replaces the dead king.

claims.claim: a cruel sceptre spreads darkness over the land

291.reading: Under his tall pearl-hung umbrella, the king of the bow and the horse-drawn chariot, having fought with sharp sword and gem shield, bearing on his head the lotus feet of the Jina and smeared with mantra-sandal, guarded by spear-eyed women, goes and becomes a guest of the gods.
291.nuance: The spear-eyed women who guard his body may be his own or the women of heaven. The Sangam formula of the fallen king as the gods' guest is joined to the Jina's feet as his last adornment.
291.event: Saccandan, dying in battle, goes to the world of the gods.

claims.claim: a king who dies fighting, bearing the Jina's feet and the mantra-sandal, goes as guest to the gods

292.reading: Five hundred sweet-voiced women, skilled in the arts and like dancing Rambhas, bringing flutes, lutes, gem drums and tannumai that young fingers sound, lament 'father, will you lie on the bare ground?' and lay him on his couch.
292.nuance: The instruments of his pleasures are brought to his body; பள்ளி படுத்தார் may be the bier or a last ritual laying out.
292.event: The king's five hundred women lament and lay out his body.

293.reading: As if silver-leafed spears and arrows pierced them, the women beat their breasts like gem caskets, their tears flowing and their loosened hair soaked in the smell of flesh, and wail like lightning in pouring rain.
293.event: The women beat their breasts and wail over the king.

links.note: Vijayai dreamed that the asoka tree fell and was utterly gone; in 289 the king falls to the earth and goes out like the setting sun.
links.teaches: The half of the dream the king refused to read at 225 is fulfilled in his fall, so the battle is the dream's first image enacted and Civakan, the shoot, is still to come.

links.note: The பிண்டி whose fall in the dream meant the king's death is in 271 the tree of the Jina whose scripture the king offers his wife as consolation.
links.teaches: One tree carries both the loss and the remedy: the royal asoka falls, and the Jina's asoka stands as the ground for not grieving that fall.

links.note: In 281 the discus cuts the king's shield as the snake joins the sun's disc; in 290 the minister is the great snake that swallows the king, sun of the Kuru line.
links.teaches: The eclipse simile moves from the shield to the man, so a battle image becomes the narrator's verdict that the usurpation is a swallowing of the sun.

links.note: In 259 Kattiyankaran proposed that the king go to rule heaven as lord of the gods; in 291 the king does go to the gods, as their guest.
links.teaches: The usurper's euphemism for murder comes literally true, but the narrator gives the king the heaven of a warrior and a Jain devotee, not the throne the usurper mockingly offered.

links.note: 261 makes the king's surrender of his army in pleasure the opening for the treachery; 290 mourns him as the sun of the just sceptre swallowed by the minister alone.
links.teaches: In death the narrator moves the blame wholly onto the usurper, so the epic holds both a negligent king and a righteous one and lets the lament forget the first.

links.note: The couplet says a ruler who does not attend and judge perishes by himself; Saccandan, who gave up rule for pleasure, perishes, but by a minister's treachery, and is mourned as just.
links.teaches: The epic splits the couplet's single cause: neglect opens the door and another's crime walks through, so the ruin is self-made in the Kural's sense yet not self-inflicted.

gains.a: the lament gains a standard that names the king's own share in his fall, which 290 leaves unsaid
gains.b: the couplet's bare தானே கெடும் gains a mechanism, the trusted minister through whom a neglectful king's ruin actually comes

links.note: Puram 62 ends with the gods of the unfading flowers receiving many guests from a field where two kings died; 291 says the dead king became a guest of the gods, adding the Jina's feet and the mantra-sandal.
links.teaches: The Jain epic keeps the Sangam honour of the fallen king as heaven's guest but makes devotion to the Jina part of his passage, so the warrior's heaven is re-founded on religion.

gains.a: the epic's phrase is shown to be the old battlefield honour, which explains why a negligent king's end can still be glorious
gains.b: the Puram formula, which grounds heaven in fighting alone, is shown being given a religious condition by a later school

links.note: Pattinathar asks how many mothers, wives, children and births he has had and has yet to have, and cries to the lord of Ekambam; Saccandan reckons births past the sands of the shore and tells his wife kinship lasts two days.
links.teaches: The same reckoning of countless births and passing kin brings the Siddhar to despair and a cry for Siva's help, and brings the Jain king to composure with no god, so the argument's outcome turns on where release is placed.

gains.a: the king's consolation is shown to be the renouncer's argument, turned to comfort a wife at a parting rather than to leave the world
gains.b: the Siddhar's anguished count gains a reader who draws calm from it through scripture, the answer his song looks for only in the Lord

source_issues: Verses 270 to 277, 286 and 290 to 293 were printed in eight half-lines and joined into four by the build (FLAG repaired); the joins read correctly.
Verse 271 line 3 விம் உயிர்த்து looks like a mis-division of விம்மு உயிர்த்து; verse 284 line 4 மிறைக்கொளி and verse 276 line 4 கயில் அணி are obscure as printed.
The prince is குருசில் in 274 and 275 and குரிசில் in 277; both spellings occur.
The enemy lord who throws the discus and spear in 280 to 283 is unnamed (அண்ணல்); identifying him with Kattiyankaran, named in 285, is a reading of the sequence.
Earlier chapter files use two ids for the usurper, kattiyangaran (ch001, ch011) and kattiyankaran (ch010, ch012); this file follows ch012.
